text.p: Britain's leading stock market index continued to defy the sceptics on Wednesday, surging towards the magical 5,000-point level despite the twin stumbling blocks of rising interest rates and strong sterling.

Just days after a poll of institutional investors revealed the most negative view towards UK equities for a year, the blue chip index jumped to an all-time best of 4,970.1, bringing its year-to-date advance to 21 percent.

It is often said that bull markets "climb a wall of worry," yet the market's sharp rise -- led by strong gains in heavyweight stocks such as Glaxo and HSBC Holdings -- has still shocked many market participants.
"One is slightly at a loss for words," said Nick Knight, London-based investment strategist at the Japanese brokerage Nomura.
"It would not appear to be fundamentally justified but this is a very powerful move and it would be extremely rash to deny it...one has to be careful about writing it off as madness."

The market's strong gains came despite last week's quarter point interest rate rise by the Bank of England, making Britain the only major economy in Europe or the U.S. to be under the cosh of higher borrowing costs.
As if to confirm the stock market's bleak outlook, a Merrill Lynch poll showed that fund managers swung to their most positive stance on gilts in two-and-a-half years.
The monthly poll of 56 institutions, which control funds totalling 775 billion stg, found that sellers outnumbered buyers by 18 percent for UK equities.
Maybe institutions were saying one thing and doing another, because the FTSE 100's upward charge has continued unabated.
Pushed for an explanation, participants noted that the FTSE 100 could appear better value than other markets having underperformed for much of this year.
Equally rates could be near their peak and inflation may stay relatively subdued, providing a benign economic backdrop through 1998.
Add in a touch of bid speculation in the banks and other sectors and the recipe for continued stock market gains seemed complete.
Yet some said the market's prime motor was more prosaic -- being simply the a high level of cash held by institutional investors.
Fund managers were sitting on a high level of cash when the market started to take off after the new Labour government's first budget on July 2.
Once they started buying, it created a shortage of shares in the big-cap companies, such as the banks, pharmaceuticals and oil companies.

"There is certainly talk about 5,000 (on the FTSE 100)," one market-maker said. "I doubt we will see it today but there is still bid talk going on, there is cash around and with any more corporate news, then it will be off to the races. This is a major squeeze."
Indeed, many participants have been left dazed and confused by the market's ebullience.
A sharp rise in sterling to 6-1/2 year highs against the German mark has proved especially problematic for big industrial companies that export to Europe.
Analysts have already downgraded their profit estimates for companies such as Imperial Chemical Industries Plc and British Steel Plc because of the risk of weaker profits overseas.
It's also worth pointing out that the FTSE 250 index of mid-ranking stocks has missed out on the FTSE 100's rally and is about flat from its price at the start of 1997.

Exacerbating sterling's rise are expectations for further interest rate hikes in the near term, after the hike in the base rate to 6.75 percent last week -- one reason Lehman Brothers has lowered its year-end target for the FTSE 100 from 5,000 to 4,800.
But Ian Scott, Lehman's European equities strategist, said the UK market was still attractive on a long-term basis, considering its position relative to other European markets.
"I think if one pointed to excessive optimism in the UK market, it is less apparent here than in the continental European markets," he said.
Some strategists said the pessimism in UK equities following the new Labour government's budget on July 2, in fact, may prove to be a good contrarian indicator.
Either way, many dealers have been hit by the market's unexpected strength and were reluctant to take a negative view.
"Sometime we will see a violent correction but the market could be 10 percent higher before that happens," said one dealer.
"We have been bearish and we have been burnt and I don't want to get caught short again."
